opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to the fact that a lot of the most important questions in AI right now are, at their core, philosophical questions — what does it mean for a system to be aligned with human values, what even are values, whose preferences count, how do we handle disagreement and uncertainty about what's good. Philosophers have been thinking carefully about these things for a very long time, and there's a rich body of work on, say, the nature of preferences, on moral uncertainty, on social choice and contractualism. But that work often lives in a vocabulary and a set of venues that people building AI systems don't really engage with.

Meanwhile, on the technical side, a lot of implicit philosophical commitments get baked into our systems without anyone quite noticing. For example, the assumption that human values can be adequately represented as a scalar reward function, or that the right thing to do is to maximize the satisfaction of revealed preferences. Those are substantive positions, and there are well-developed critiques of them, but if you don't have the conceptual tools to see them as choices, they just look like the default way to set up the problem.

So for me, translation goes both ways. Part of it is taking ideas from philosophy and making them precise enough — sometimes literally formalizing them, in terms of probabilistic models or decision theory — that engineers can see how they'd change what we build. And part of it is helping philosophers see where the technical constraints actually bite, so the conversation is grounded. I come from a background where I care a lot about both, and I've found that a lot of confusion in AI alignment debates comes from people talking past each other because they lack that shared language. If I can help build some of that bridge, I think we end up with systems that are more thoughtful about what they're actually trying to do on our behalf.

r001.rationale: The response says philosophical work often uses vocabulary and venues that AI builders do not engage with, and that translation can make the ideas accessible to engineers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it matters because a lot of the people actually building these systems are making philosophical commitments without quite realizing it. When you write down a reward function, or you decide what counts as "the user's preferences," or you say a model should be "aligned with human values," you've already taken a position on questions that philosophers have been arguing about for centuries. What is a preference? Is it the same thing as what someone would endorse on reflection? Whose values, and how do you aggregate them when people disagree?

And the thing is, there's an enormous amount of careful thinking already out there on those questions. Decision theory, moral philosophy, philosophy of action, social choice. But it's written in a vocabulary that doesn't map cleanly onto loss functions and training pipelines, so it tends to get ignored, or worse, reinvented badly. I've seen papers essentially rediscover a critique of preference utilitarianism from the 1970s and present it as a novel observation about RLHF.

So part of what I try to do is act as a translator. Take an argument from the philosophy side and say, here's what this actually implies for your modeling assumptions, here's the concrete case where your formalism breaks. And in the other direction, take the technical constraints seriously and push back on philosophical frameworks that are elegant but can't be implemented in anything you'd actually deploy.

I also just think the stakes make it important. If we're building systems that will mediate a lot of human decision-making, the conceptual foundations really shouldn't be an afterthought. Getting the philosophy slightly wrong at the design stage can propagate into every downstream system. So I'd rather the people with their hands on the levers have access to the best thinking available, in a form they can actually use.

r001.rationale: The response says philosophical work is often written in vocabulary that does not map cleanly onto technical workflows, so technical audiences ignore it or reinvent its ideas.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of technical work on AI involves philosophical questions, whether we acknowledge them or not. What does it mean to understand someone’s preferences? What counts as acting in their interests? Those aren’t questions that an optimization algorithm can settle for us. They shape what we choose to optimize in the first place.

So translating between those conversations matters because philosophy can help us see assumptions that otherwise get buried in a technical formulation. And technical work can push us to make philosophical ideas more precise: What would this view actually imply for how we build a system? Where does it break down?

The goal isn’t necessarily to get everyone to agree on one philosophical position. It’s to give people the concepts to recognize that there are choices here, and to reason more carefully about the consequences of those choices.

r001.rationale: The response says translating matters because philosophy surfaces hidden assumptions and technical work can sharpen ideas, but it does not identify insufficient translation as a reason philosophical ideas fail to reach technical audiences.

sol-6.1.text:
I think technical work often contains philosophical assumptions, whether or not we make them explicit. When we talk about an AI system having goals, understanding something, or aligning with human values, we’re already using concepts that philosophers have spent a long time trying to clarify.

For me, translating between those conversations is about making the assumptions visible and useful. What do we mean by a goal? What would count as understanding? Where might different interpretations lead us to build different systems? You don’t necessarily need to settle every philosophical debate, but understanding the distinctions can help you ask better technical questions.

r001.rationale: The response says translation can make philosophical assumptions visible and useful, but does not state that insufficient translation is why many philosophical ideas fail to reach technical audiences.
